learn.title: Bounds from below and tight
learn.body: Big O is an upper bound: the work grows no faster than this. Two partners complete it. Omega, written $\Omega$, is a lower bound: the work grows at least this fast. Theta, written $\Theta$, is a tight bound: both at once.

learn.title: In plain words
learn.body: $O(f)$ means at most that growth. $\Omega(f)$ means at least that growth. $\Theta(f)$ means at least and at most, so the shape is exactly $f$. When someone says an algorithm is $\Theta(n)$ they promise it never grows much slower or faster than a line.

learn.title: The max-finder is theta of n
learn.body: Recall the loop that finds the largest value.
steps: It compares each of the other n - 1 items once
It never stops early, whatever the values are
So it always does n - 1 comparisons, which is $\Theta(n)$
It is also $O(n)$ and $\Omega(n)$, since theta means both

learn.title: Bounds can be loose
learn.body: Every $\Theta(n)$ code is also $O(n^2)$, because n never grows faster than $n^2$. That is true but not helpful. Use the tightest bound you can prove. A loose bound is correct but tells you little.
Many people say big O when they mean the tight bound. When it matters, ask whether $\Theta$ is what is meant.

questions.prompt: Which symbol means a lower bound?
questions.explanation: Omega says the work grows at least this fast.

questions.prompt: Which symbol means a tight bound?
questions.explanation: Theta means both an upper and a lower bound.

questions.prompt: Code that always does exactly $n - 1$ comparisons is \_\_.
questions.explanation: The count is a line in n at both ends, so the tight bound is theta of n.

questions.prompt: A loop always runs `n` times, with no early exit. Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Always n steps means at least n and at most n. That is $\Theta(n)$.

questions.prompt: Match each symbol to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Theta is the pair of upper and lower bound together.

choices: Yes, as a loose upper bound
questions.explanation: Linear growth is no faster than quadratic, so the bound holds. It is just not tight.

questions.prompt: The max-finder on 10 items makes how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: It compares each of the other items once, so n - 1 = 9.
